metric_rationale: By restricting the analysis to subsets of trials where Tallying computes the exact same score difference (e.g., A wins exactly 1 more feature than B), Tallying predicts a constant probability of choosing A across those trials. However, WADD uses the validities and cardinal feature magnitudes, so it still predicts variation in choice probabilities within these subsets. The metric computes the difference in the empirical probability of choosing A between the trials WADD strongly favors and the trials WADD weakly favors, holding the Tallying score difference strictly constant. This yields an expected value of 0 for Tallying and a positive value for WADD.

In Trial 8, Option A is better on the lowest-validity feature while Option B is better on the highest-validity feature. Tallying ignores validities and counts this as a 1-1 tie, predicting a 50% chance of choosing either option. WADD weights the features by their validities, so it strongly prefers Option B. The metric measures the proportion of times Option B is chosen on this specific trial, which cleanly discriminates the two theories.

This metric isolates the specific 'compensatory' trials in the design where the most valid cue (F1) favors one option, but a combination of lower-validity cues favors the other option. On these trials, Take The Best strictly predicts choosing the option with the highest valid cue, while Weighted Additive (WADD) can compensate and choose the other option. By calculating the proportion of choices that align with the TTB prediction on these specific trials, we expect TTB to score close to 1.0 (minus noise), whereas WADD will score significantly lower as it frequently chooses the compensatory option.

This metric isolates trials (10 and 14) where the two theories make opposing predictions. On these trials, one option has a singular advantage on the second-most valid feature (validity 0.94), while the other option has advantages on both the third and fourth features (validities 0.66 and 0.55). TTB, being lexicographic, will always choose the option with the advantage on the higher-validity single feature. WADD, being compensatory, will frequently evaluate the combined weight of the two lesser features as exceeding the single higher-validity feature, leading to the opposite choice. The metric returns the proportion of choices that align with the compensatory (WADD) prediction.

Take The Best (TTB) uses only the first discriminating feature, ignoring the rest. Because it just assigns a binary 1/0 score to the winner/loser regardless of how many features support the choice or the validity of the deciding feature, TTB's predicted choice probability is identical across all trials (modulo noise). In contrast, Rank-Weighted Additive Theory (RWAT) accumulates evidence across all features, producing a large score difference when all features align (Trial 14) and a very small score difference when only the lowest-ranked feature discriminates (Trial 7). Thus, the difference in accuracy between Trial 14 and Trial 7 will be exactly 0 under TTB, but significantly greater than 0 under RWAT.

Take The Best (TTB) uses a strict lexicographic rule. It decides based solely on the highest-validity cue that discriminates the options, completely ignoring any opposing lower-validity cues. Therefore, the probability of choosing the option favored by the best cue should be identical regardless of how many lower cues oppose it. Rank-Weighted Additive (RWA) integrates all cues using a decaying weight scheme. Thus, when multiple lower-validity cues oppose the highest-validity cue, the evidence margin shrinks, pulling the choice probability towards 0.5. By taking the difference in choice probabilities between trials with strong opposition vs. weak/no opposition, TTB will predict a difference near zero, whereas RWA will predict a significantly positive difference.
